question: IT company: CFO 10,000cr, D&A 2,000cr, Capex 1,500cr. Capex < D&A suggests:
before: For IT, primary asset is human capital (P&L cost), not physical assets. Capex/D&A slightly below 1.0x is normal because D&A includes software amortisation and ROU assets. For steel or cement, capex < D&A would indicate underinvestment. Context matters.
after:
Concept: The relationship between Capex and D&A signals whether a company is maintaining, building, or harvesting its asset base. Capex < D&A means cash outflow for new assets is less than the non-cash charge for depreciation and amortisation — a pattern whose interpretation depends critically on the business model.

Why this is correct: IT companies are asset-light businesses where the primary value driver is human capital and intellectual property, not physical infrastructure. D&A of ₹2,000 cr includes not only physical plant depreciation but also software amortisation and right-of-use (ROU) asset amortisation under Ind-AS 116. Capex of ₹1,500 cr represents actual spend on servers, offices, and equipment — which for a mature IT services firm generating ₹10,000 cr in operating cash flow is adequate to maintain and incrementally upgrade the asset base. A ratio of Capex/D&A = 75% is normal and healthy for this sector, not a red flag.

Why the others are wrong: A) Underinvesting is a misdiagnosis because it ignores the asset-light nature of IT and conflates Capex < D&A with distress — a pattern that applies only to capital-intensive industries. C) Demanding higher capex would be value-destructive because IT companies generate superior returns on incremental capex due to leverage of intellectual property; pushing capex above D&A would dilute ROIC and tie up cash unnecessarily. D) Both A and C compounds both errors — it treats the normal IT profile as a problem requiring correction.

Intuition: In equity research, always contextualise Capex/D&A within industry norms and the nature of the competitive advantage. For asset-heavy cyclicals (steel, cement, infrastructure), Capex < D&A signals fleet decay and underinvestment. For asset-light, high-margin businesses (IT, software, consulting), low Capex intensity relative to D&A is a marker of capital efficiency and sustainable economics — exactly what drives superior long-term returns.
